title: Homo sapiens at Jebel Irhoud
summary: Fossil skulls at Jebel Irhoud are widely dated to about 300,000 years ago and are among the oldest known Homo sapiens. They combine a modern-looking face with a more archaic braincase. The finds place our species in north-west Africa by about 300,000 years ago.
dateNote: Approximate. The fossils are widely dated to about 300,000 years ago.

title: Homo naledi in the Rising Star caves
summary: Homo naledi is a small-brained hominin known from a deep cave system north-west of Johannesburg. The remains are dated to roughly 335,000 to 236,000 years ago, so the later part of that span falls within the last 300,000 years. How the bodies entered the chamber is still debated.
dateNote: Approximate. The published age is about 335,000 to 236,000 years ago.

title: Omo Kibish fossils
summary: Fossils from the Kibish Formation near the Omo River are among the oldest widely accepted Homo sapiens remains in eastern Africa. A 2022 study dated the deposits to at least about 233,000 years ago. They show that people with modern anatomy were in the Rift Valley long before later dispersals.
dateNote: Approximate. The deposits are dated to at least about 233,000 years ago.

title: Herto humans
summary: Skulls from Herto in the Afar are widely dated to about 160,000 to 154,000 years ago. They are often classed as Homo sapiens idaltu, an early form of our species. Cut marks on one skull have been read as signs of mortuary practice, though that reading is cautious.
dateNote: Approximate. The skulls are widely dated to about 160,000 to 154,000 years ago.

title: Engraved ochre at Blombos Cave
summary: Blombos Cave has engraved ochre pieces and shell beads dated to roughly 77,000 to 73,000 years ago. The cross-hatched ochre is among the oldest widely accepted marks made as a design. The beads suggest that people were already using ornaments.
dateNote: Approximate. The objects are dated to about 77,000 to 73,000 years ago.

title: Painted slabs from Apollo 11 Cave
summary: Seven painted stone slabs from Apollo 11 Cave in southern Namibia are among the oldest known paintings in Africa. They are widely dated to about 25,000 to 27,000 years ago. The images include animals painted on loose stones rather than on the cave wall.
dateNote: Approximate. The slabs are widely dated to about 25,000 to 27,000 years ago.

title: Out of Africa
summary: Genetic and archaeological evidence points to a major dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa roughly 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. People moved through the Horn and into southern Asia over many generations. The line is a schematic of that southern route, not a single journey.
dateNote: Approximate. The main dispersal is widely placed at about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago.

title: Bantu expansion
summary: Speakers of Bantu languages spread from the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands into central, eastern, and southern Africa. The movement is widely placed from about 1000 BCE into the early centuries CE, and it carried farming and, later, ironworking. The line is a schematic of the main branches, not one migration.
dateNote: Approximate. The expansion is widely dated from about 1000 BCE into the early first millennium CE.

title: Unification of Egypt
summary: Late predynastic objects, including the Narmer Palette, depict a ruler of Upper Egypt subduing the north. Egypt was joined into one kingdom around 3100 BCE, with Abydos an early royal cemetery. The exact year and the role of one king named Narmer remain approximate.
dateNote: Approximate. Unification is widely placed around 3100 BCE.

title: Early writing in Mesopotamia
summary: At Uruk, clay tablets with pictographic signs appear in the late fourth millennium BCE. They tracked goods and labour, and they developed into cuneiform. The tablets belong to the centuries just before and around 3000 BCE.
dateNote: Approximate. The earliest tablets are widely dated to about 3400–3000 BCE.

title: Great Pyramid of Khufu
summary: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for the king Khufu in the Fourth Dynasty. It is widely dated to the decades around 2580–2560 BCE. It remained the tallest human structure for most of later history.
dateNote: Approximate. Khufu's reign is widely placed in the 26th century BCE.

title: Kingdom of Kerma
summary: Kerma, on the Nile in Nubia, was a powerful city-state trading and at times fighting with Egypt. Its classic phase is widely dated to about 2500–1500 BCE. Huge earthen tumuli at the site mark its rulers.
dateNote: Approximate. The classic Kerma kingdom is widely dated to about 2500–1500 BCE.

title: Reign of Hatshepsut
summary: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as pharaoh in the early Eighteenth Dynasty and built a terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri. Her reign is widely dated to about 1479–1458 BCE. Reliefs there record an expedition to Punt, somewhere on the Red Sea coast of Africa.
dateNote: Approximate. Her reign is widely dated to about 1479–1458 BCE.

title: Akhenaten's new capital
summary: Akhenaten promoted the cult of the Aten and founded a new capital at Amarna. His reign is widely placed in the mid-fourteenth century BCE. After his death the court returned to Thebes and the experiment was abandoned.
dateNote: Approximate. The Amarna period is widely placed in the mid-fourteenth century BCE.

title: Reign of Ramesses II
summary: Ramesses II ruled Egypt for much of the thirteenth century BCE and built on a huge scale, including Abu Simbel. His reign is widely dated to about 1279–1213 BCE. He also fought the Hittites at Kadesh and later made a treaty with them.
dateNote: Approximate. His reign is widely dated to about 1279–1213 BCE.

title: Merneptah Stele
summary: A victory inscription of the pharaoh Merneptah, dated to about 1208 BCE, lists a people called Israel in Canaan. It is the earliest widely accepted mention of that name. The text celebrates Egyptian campaigns, not a history of Israel itself.
dateNote: The stele is widely dated to Merneptah's fifth year, about 1208 BCE.

title: Nok culture
summary: The Nok culture of central Nigeria produced distinctive terracotta figures and, later, iron. It is widely dated from about 1500 BCE to the early centuries CE, with iron well established by the mid-first millennium BCE. Many of the sculptures were found in tin mines.
dateNote: Approximate. Nok terracottas and ironworking are widely placed from about 1500 BCE onward.

title: Kushite kings in Egypt
summary: Kings from Kush, centred at Napata, conquered Egypt in the eighth century BCE and ruled as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. Their rule there is widely dated to about 747–656 BCE. They were later pushed back up the Nile by Assyrian campaigns.
dateNote: Approximate. The Kushite dynasty in Egypt is widely dated to about 747–656 BCE.

title: Royal city of Meroë
summary: Meroë became the royal centre of Kush and a major ironworking city. Its heyday runs from about the third century BCE to the fourth century CE. Rulers, including reigning queens, were buried under steep pyramids nearby.
dateNote: Approximate. Meroë's royal period is widely placed from about 300 BCE to 350 CE.

title: Carthage and Rome
summary: Carthage, a Phoenician foundation in what is now Tunisia, fought three wars with Rome between 264 and 146 BCE. Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE after the Third Punic War. The traditional foundation date of 814 BCE is less secure than these war years.
dateNote: The Punic Wars are dated from 264 to 146 BCE.

title: Death of Cleopatra
summary: Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemaic ruler of Egypt, died in 30 BCE after Rome defeated her and Mark Antony. Egypt then became a Roman province. Ancient accounts of the manner of her death differ in their details.
dateNote: Her death is dated to 30 BCE.

title: Ezana of Aksum
summary: Ezana ruled the kingdom of Aksum in the fourth century and issued inscriptions and coins. During his reign the court adopted Christianity. Aksum controlled Red Sea trade and, for a time, parts of southern Arabia.
dateNote: Approximate. Ezana's reign is widely placed in the mid-fourth century CE.

title: Kingdom of Ghana
summary: The kingdom called Ghana by Arab writers dominated the savanna trade in gold and salt. Its height is widely placed between about 800 and 1100. The capital is often identified with Koumbi Saleh, though that identification is not certain.
dateNote: Approximate. Arab geographers describe the kingdom in these centuries.

title: Kilwa and the Swahili coast
summary: Stone towns along the East African coast, linked by the Swahili language, traded gold, ivory, and timber across the Indian Ocean. Kilwa was a leading port from about the eleventh to the fifteenth century. Its Great Mosque still stands.
dateNote: Approximate. Kilwa's peak is widely placed between about 1000 and 1500.

title: Rock churches of Lalibela
summary: Churches cut from living rock at Lalibela are traditionally linked to the Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela. They are widely dated to around the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries. The town remains a major Christian pilgrimage site.
dateNote: Approximate. The churches are widely dated to about 1180–1220.

title: Founding of the Mali Empire
summary: Sundiata Keita defeated the Soso king Sumanguru at the battle of Kirina, widely placed in about 1235, and built the Mali Empire. Mali then controlled long-distance trade across the western savanna. The epic told about Sundiata is a later oral tradition.
dateNote: Approximate. Kirina is widely placed in about 1235.

title: Great Zimbabwe
summary: Great Zimbabwe was the stone-built capital of a Shona kingdom that traded gold to the Indian Ocean coast. Its main occupation is widely dated from about the eleventh to the fifteenth century. The site was built by local African masons, a point long established by archaeology.
dateNote: Approximate. The stone city flourished from about 1100 to 1450.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
summary: Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, travelled to Mecca in 1324–1325 and passed through Cairo with a very large supply of gold. Contemporary writers in Egypt described the journey and its effect on the gold market. He also sponsored mosques and learning in Timbuktu.
dateNote: The hajj is dated to 1324–1325.

title: Songhai takes Timbuktu
summary: Sunni Ali of Songhai took Timbuktu in 1468 and expanded a empire along the Niger bend. The city stayed a centre of manuscript learning under Songhai rule. Moroccan forces later defeated Songhai in 1591.
dateNote: Sunni Ali's capture of Timbuktu is dated to 1468.

title: Kongo meets Portugal
summary: Portuguese ships reached the kingdom of Kongo in 1483, and King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised in 1491. The contact began a long and unequal relationship, including the trade in enslaved people. Kongo remained an independent kingdom for centuries after.
dateNote: The first Portuguese embassy is dated to 1483, and the royal baptism to 1491.

title: Walls of Benin City
summary: The kingdom of Benin built a vast system of earth walls and ditches around its capital and the surrounding landscape. Much of the monumental work is dated to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Brass plaques from the court, later looted in 1897, record its history.
dateNote: Approximate. The major earthworks are widely placed in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

title: Sokoto Caliphate
summary: Usman dan Fodio led a jihad from 1804 that overthrew Hausa rulers and founded the Sokoto Caliphate. By 1808 the new state was the largest in West Africa. It lasted until British conquest in the early twentieth century.
dateNote: The jihad began in 1804.

title: Rise of the Zulu kingdom
summary: Shaka kaSenzangakhona built a centralised Zulu kingdom in the late 1810s and 1820s. The wars of that period reshaped societies across southern Africa. Many vivid details in later biographies of Shaka are disputed, but the rise of the kingdom is not.
dateNote: Approximate. Shaka's reign is widely placed from about 1816 to 1828.

title: Decipherment of hieroglyphs
summary: In 1822 Jean-François Champollion announced that he could read ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, using the Rosetta Stone and other bilingual texts. The decipherment opened three thousand years of Egyptian writing to modern study. The stone itself had been found by French soldiers in 1799.
dateNote: Champollion's letter to Dacier is dated 27 September 1822.

title: Independence of Liberia
summary: Settlers from the United States declared the Republic of Liberia in 1847. The new state was not ruled by a European colonial power, but it also excluded many indigenous people from power. Its capital was named for the American president James Monroe.
dateNote: Independence was declared on 26 July 1847.

title: Battle of Adwa
summary: On 1 March 1896 Ethiopian armies under Emperor Menelik II defeated an Italian invasion at Adwa. The victory preserved Ethiopian independence during the European partition of Africa. It became a symbol for later anti-colonial movements.
dateNote: The battle was fought on 1 March 1896.

title: Looting of Benin City
summary: In 1897 a British punitive expedition burned Benin City and seized thousands of royal plaques and sculptures. The objects were sold to museums and collectors in Europe. Many are now the subject of return claims by Nigeria.
dateNote: The expedition took the city in February 1897.

title: Genocide of the Herero and Nama
summary: From 1904 German colonial troops crushed Herero and Nama resistance in what is now Namibia. People were driven into the desert and survivors were held in camps. The campaign is widely recognised as a genocide.
dateNote: The war and the camps are dated to 1904–1908.

title: Maji Maji uprising
summary: In 1905 people across southern German East Africa rose against forced cotton growing and colonial rule. The uprising, called Maji Maji, was defeated by 1907. Famine that followed the German scorched-earth response killed very large numbers.
dateNote: The uprising is dated to 1905–1907.

title: Italian invasion of Ethiopia
summary: Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935 and occupied Addis Ababa in May 1936. Emperor Haile Selassie appealed to the League of Nations, which failed to stop the conquest. Ethiopian and Allied forces drove the Italians out in 1941.
dateNote: The invasion began on 3 October 1935.

title: Apartheid government
summary: In 1948 the National Party won power in South Africa and extended racial segregation into the system called apartheid. Later laws classified people by race and forced millions into separate areas. The system lasted until the election of 1994.
dateNote: The National Party took office after the election of 26 May 1948.

title: Independence of Ghana
summary: The Gold Coast became independent Ghana on 6 March 1957, with Kwame Nkrumah as prime minister. It was the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from European rule in that wave. Nkrumah made Accra a centre of pan-African politics.
dateNote: Independence was declared on 6 March 1957.

title: Year of Africa
summary: In 1960 seventeen African countries became independent, most of them from France. The year is often called the Year of Africa. It marked the rapid end of formal colonial rule across much of the continent.
dateNote: Seventeen independences fell in the calendar year 1960.

title: Sharpeville massacre
summary: On 21 March 1960 police fired on a crowd protesting pass laws at Sharpeville, killing 69 people. The government then banned the African National Congress and the Pan Africanist Congress. The date is now honoured as Human Rights Day in South Africa.
dateNote: The shooting was on 21 March 1960.

title: Independence of Algeria
summary: A war against French rule ran from 1954 until the Evian Accords of 1962. Algeria declared independence on 5 July 1962 after a referendum. The war killed very large numbers of Algerians and ended more than 130 years of French colonisation.
dateNote: Independence was proclaimed on 5 July 1962.

title: Nigerian Civil War
summary: The Eastern Region seceded as Biafra in 1967, and the Nigerian federal government fought to restore the union until 1970. A blockade caused a famine that was seen around the world. Biafra surrendered in January 1970.
dateNote: The war is dated from 6 July 1967 to 15 January 1970.

title: Soweto uprising
summary: On 16 June 1976 students in Soweto marched against schooling in Afrikaans. Police opened fire, and the protests spread across South Africa. The uprising is often marked by the photograph of the dying Hector Pieterson, aged twelve.
dateNote: The march was on 16 June 1976.

title: Discovery of Lucy
summary: In 1974 a team at Hadar found a partial skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis, nicknamed Lucy. The fossil itself is about 3.2 million years old, far older than the last 300,000 years. The discovery changed the public picture of early human ancestors.
dateNote: The skeleton was found on 24 November 1974. The fossil is much older than 300,000 BCE.

title: Election of Nelson Mandela
summary: South Africa held its first election with universal adult suffrage in April 1994, and Nelson Mandela became president. The vote ended formal apartheid. Mandela had been released from prison in 1990 after 27 years.
dateNote: The election was held on 27 April 1994.

title: Genocide against the Tutsi
summary: Between April and July 1994 extremists in Rwanda organised the murder of hundreds of thousands of Tutsi, and of Hutu who opposed the killing. The genocide unfolded in about one hundred days while a civil war continued. An international tribunal later judged the killings a genocide.
dateNote: The genocide is dated from 7 April to mid-July 1994.

title: Independence of South Sudan
summary: After a long civil war and a 2011 referendum, South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011. It was the newest widely recognised state in Africa. A further civil war began inside the country in 2013.
dateNote: Independence was on 9 July 2011.

title: Tunisian revolution
summary: Protests beginning in December 2010 forced President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali from office in January 2011. The uprising started a wave of revolts across the Arab world. Tunisia later adopted a new constitution, though politics remained contested.
dateNote: Ben Ali left office on 14 January 2011.

title: Myth of Osiris
summary: Osiris, killed and restored as ruler of the dead, is a central figure of Egyptian religion and is especially tied to Abydos. The story is already present in the Pyramid Texts of the Old Kingdom. Later tellings, including Plutarch's, are much younger than those inscriptions.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The Pyramid Texts, from about the 24th century BCE, already refer to Osiris.

title: Creation at Ile-Ife
summary: Yoruba tradition places the creation of the world and the first kingship at Ile-Ife. The oral religion is far older than any book. Substantial written accounts of these traditions were set down by Yoruba and European authors in the nineteenth century.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Nineteenth-century writers recorded traditions that are much older.

title: Epic of Sundiata
summary: Griots have long told the epic of Sundiata, the founder of Mali, blending a thirteenth-century ruler with marvels and prophecy. The historical founding of Mali is a separate historical episode. Full versions of the epic were written down from oral performance in the twentieth century.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Widely circulated written versions were recorded from oral performance in the twentieth century. The tradition is medieval.

title: Epic of Mwindo
summary: The Nyanga epic of Mwindo tells of a miraculous child who quarrels with his father and travels to the realm of the gods. It was an oral tradition until Daniel Biebuyck recorded performances and published them. The story belongs to the Nyanga people of the eastern Congo forests.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Biebuyck's publications of the 1950s and 1960s are the first full written texts. The oral epic is older.

title: Hearths at Qesem Cave
summary: Qesem Cave has repeated hearths and butchered animal bones from the later Middle Pleistocene. The cave's deposits begin earlier than 300,000 years ago and continue to about 200,000 years ago. They are widely cited as evidence of habitual fire use by early humans in the Levant.
dateNote: Approximate. The later hearths fall between about 300,000 and 200,000 years ago.

title: Early humans at Skhul and Qafzeh
summary: Burials at Skhul and Qafzeh show Homo sapiens in the Levant about 120,000 to 90,000 years ago. This early presence outside Africa may not have lasted. A later dispersal, after about 70,000 years ago, is the one that peopled the rest of the world.
dateNote: Approximate. The burials are widely dated to about 120,000–90,000 years ago.

title: Toba eruption
summary: The Toba supervolcano in Sumatra erupted about 74,000 years ago, the largest known eruption of the last two million years. Ash from it is found across South Asia. Claims that it almost wiped out humanity are now widely doubted.
dateNote: Approximate. The eruption is widely dated to about 74,000 years ago.

title: Denisovans of the Altai
summary: A finger bone and teeth from Denisova Cave belonged to a population now called Denisovans, known mainly from ancient DNA. Fossils from the cave span a broad period around 100,000 to 50,000 years ago, and individual dates still differ. People today in Island Southeast Asia and Oceania carry some Denisovan ancestry.
dateNote: Approximate. The cave's Denisovan fossils fall broadly between about 100,000 and 50,000 years ago.

title: Homo floresiensis
summary: Remains of a small-bodied hominin, nicknamed the hobbit, were found at Liang Bua on Flores. Revised dating places the bones at about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, not in the last 12,000 years as first reported. The species shows that several kinds of human lived in Island Southeast Asia.
dateNote: Approximate. The revised chronology places the bones at about 100,000–60,000 years ago.

title: Cave painting in Sulawesi
summary: A painting of a warty pig at Leang Tedongnge is dated to at least 45,500 years ago. It is among the oldest known figurative art in the world. Nearby caves in Maros-Pangkep have other paintings of a similar age.
dateNote: Approximate. The pig painting is dated to at least about 45,500 years ago.

title: Jōmon pottery
summary: Pottery of the Incipient Jōmon tradition is among the oldest known anywhere. Early vessels are widely dated to about 14,000 BCE, with dates varying by site. Hunter-gatherers in the Japanese archipelago made and used them long before farming.
dateNote: Approximate. The earliest Jōmon pots are widely placed around 14,000 BCE.

title: Göbekli Tepe
summary: At Göbekli Tepe, hunter-gatherers raised T-shaped stone pillars carved with animals. The enclosures are widely dated to about 9600–8200 BCE, before pottery and before settled farming villages in the region. The site was later deliberately buried.
dateNote: Approximate. The main enclosures are widely dated to about 9600–8200 BCE.

title: Tower of Jericho
summary: A stone tower and wall at Tell es-Sultan belong to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, around the eighth millennium BCE. Jericho is one of the longest-lived settlement mounds in the world. The tower is older than the pottery and cities of later ages.
dateNote: Approximate. The tower is widely dated to the eighth millennium BCE.

title: Çatalhöyük
summary: Çatalhöyük was a dense settlement of mud-brick houses entered from the roof. It was occupied from about 7100 to 6000 BCE. Wall paintings and burials under the floors show a rich ritual life.
dateNote: Approximate. The main occupation is widely dated to about 7100–6000 BCE.

title: Rice cultivation on the Yangtze
summary: People in the Yangtze basin domesticated rice over several thousand years. Early cultivated rice is widely in place by about 7000–5000 BCE. It later became the staple of much of East and Southeast Asia.
dateNote: Approximate. Early rice cultivation is widely placed by about 7000–5000 BCE.

title: Mehrgarh
summary: Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass, has some of the earliest farming and herding in South Asia. The first occupation is widely dated to about 7000 BCE. Later levels lead toward the Indus cities.
dateNote: Approximate. The early farming levels are widely dated from about 7000 BCE.

title: Indus cities
summary: From about 2600 to 1900 BCE, cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa shared weights, seals, and planned streets across the Indus basin. Their script is still undeciphered. The cities were largely abandoned after about 1900 BCE.
dateNote: Approximate. The mature Indus phase is widely dated to about 2600–1900 BCE.

title: Empire of Akkad
summary: Sargon of Akkad built a state that joined the cities of Mesopotamia in the twenty-fourth century BCE. Later tradition gave him a long reign, and the exact years are approximate. The empire fell in the twenty-second century BCE.
dateNote: Approximate. Sargon's reign is widely placed in the 24th century BCE.

title: Laws of Hammurabi
summary: Hammurabi, king of Babylon, set up a diorite stele of laws in the eighteenth century BCE. The prologue and epilogue frame a long list of judgments. It is one of the earliest extensive law codes to survive.
dateNote: Approximate. The stele is widely dated to Hammurabi's reign, around 1750 BCE.

title: Hittite capital at Hattusa
summary: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite kingdom, a great power of the Late Bronze Age. The city and the archives of cuneiform tablets were abandoned around 1180 BCE, during the wider Bronze Age collapse. The texts include treaties and royal annals.
dateNote: Approximate. Hattusa was a capital from about 1650 BCE until about 1180 BCE.

title: Oracle bones of Anyang
summary: At Yinxu, the late Shang capital, kings recorded divinations on cattle bone and turtle shell. These oracle bones, from about 1250 to 1046 BCE, are the earliest substantial Chinese writing. They name royal ancestors and military campaigns.
dateNote: Approximate. The Anyang oracle bones are widely dated to about 1250–1046 BCE.

title: Bronze Age collapse
summary: Around 1200–1150 BCE, palace societies from Greece to the Levant were destroyed or shrank. Ugarit, the Hittite kingdom, and Mycenaean centres fell within a few decades. The causes are still debated, and Egyptian texts mention groups they called the Sea Peoples.
dateNote: Approximate. The main destructions cluster around 1200–1150 BCE.

title: Zhou conquest of the Shang
summary: The Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye and founded a new dynasty. The traditional date used by many historians is 1046 BCE, though other ancient chronologies differ by decades. The Zhou then ruled through a network of kin domains.
dateNote: Approximate. 1046 BCE is a widely used date, and ancient chronologies disagree.

title: Phoenician alphabet
summary: By about 1050 BCE, Phoenician cities were using a short alphabet of consonants. It is the ancestor of the Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, and Latin scripts. Early examples come from Byblos and other Levantine ports.
dateNote: Approximate. The script is widely in use by about the eleventh to tenth century BCE.

title: Cyrus takes Babylon
summary: In 539 BCE Cyrus of Persia took Babylon, ending the Neo-Babylonian kingdom. The Cyrus Cylinder describes him as a restorer of temples and of displaced peoples. His empire then stretched from the Aegean to Central Asia.
dateNote: Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BCE.

title: Confucius
summary: Kong Qiu, known in the West as Confucius, taught in the state of Lu in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE. The traditional dates of his life are 551–479 BCE. The Analects, a collection of his sayings, was compiled by later followers.
dateNote: The traditional dates are 551–479 BCE.

title: The Buddha
summary: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught a path out of suffering in the kingdoms of the central Ganges. Most historians place his life in the fifth or fourth century BCE. The traditional dates used in South Asia are earlier and are not agreed.
dateNote: Approximate. His life is widely placed in the fifth or fourth century BCE.

title: Persepolis
summary: Darius I began the ceremonial capital of Persepolis in the late sixth century BCE. Reliefs there show delegations from across the Persian Empire bringing tribute. Alexander burned the palaces in 330 BCE.
dateNote: Construction began under Darius I around 518 BCE. Alexander burned the site in 330 BCE.

title: Alexander at Gaugamela
summary: In 331 BCE Alexander of Macedon defeated Darius III at Gaugamela and then took the Persian capitals. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE. His campaigns linked the eastern Mediterranean with Iran and the Indus.
dateNote: Gaugamela was fought on 1 October 331 BCE. Alexander died in 323 BCE.

title: Edicts of Ashoka
summary: Ashoka, emperor of the Maurya realm, inscribed edicts on rocks and pillars across South Asia. They are widely dated to his reign, about 268–232 BCE, and some express remorse after the war in Kalinga. The edicts are the earliest extensive royal inscriptions of India.
dateNote: Approximate. Ashoka's reign is widely dated to about 268–232 BCE.

title: Qin unification of China
summary: In 221 BCE the king of Qin conquered the last rival state and took the title First Emperor. His government standardised script, weights, and axle widths. The dynasty fell in 206 BCE, soon after his death.
dateNote: Unification is dated to 221 BCE.

title: Zhang Qian's journey
summary: The Han envoy Zhang Qian left Chang'an around 139 BCE, was held by the Xiongnu, and reached Central Asia before returning about 126 BCE. His report opened regular Han contact with the western regions. It is an early dated moment of the Silk Road.
dateNote: His mission is dated to about 139–126 BCE.

title: Silk Road
summary: From the Han period into the early centuries CE, caravan routes linked China with Central Asia, Iran, and the Mediterranean. Silk, horses, glass, and ideas moved along them, and Dunhuang became a major gateway. The line is a schematic of the main land route, not a single road.
dateNote: Approximate. The classic land routes are well attested from the late second century BCE.

title: Paper reported to the Han court
summary: In 105 CE the official Cai Lun presented an improved method of making paper to the Han emperor. Earlier plant-fibre sheets exist, so he did not invent paper from nothing. His process is the one later texts credit with spreading paper use.
dateNote: The court presentation is traditionally dated to 105 CE.

title: Three Kingdoms
summary: After the Han collapse, Wei, Shu, and Wu divided China from 220 until the Jin conquest of Wu in 280. The period is well dated in the dynastic histories. Later fiction, especially the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, added a great deal of legend.
dateNote: The kingdoms are dated from 220 to 280.

title: Gupta Empire
summary: Chandra Gupta I began the Gupta era in 320, and his successors ruled much of northern India. The period is associated with Sanskrit learning, temple building, and the mathematician Aryabhata. Hun invasions weakened the empire in the sixth century.
dateNote: The Gupta era begins in 320.

title: Sassanid Empire
summary: Ardashir I founded the Sassanid Empire in 224, and it remained the great power of Iran until the Arab conquest of 651. Its kings revived Zoroastrian state ritual and fought Rome and later Byzantium. The capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris.
dateNote: The dynasty is dated from 224 to the fall of Ctesiphon's realm in 651.

title: Hijra
summary: In 622 Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Yathrib, later called Medina. The journey, the Hijra, is year 1 of the Islamic calendar. From Medina the new community grew into a state.
dateNote: The Hijra is dated to 622.

title: Arab conquest of Sasanian Iraq
summary: Arab Muslim armies defeated Sasanian forces at Qadisiyyah around 636 and took Ctesiphon. By 651 the last Sasanian king had been killed and Iran was under the new caliphate. The exact year of the battle is still discussed.
dateNote: Approximate. Qadisiyyah is widely placed in the mid-630s, and the Sasanian realm ended by 651.

title: Foundation of Baghdad
summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad as his capital in 762, on a round plan beside the Tigris. The city became a centre of scholarship, including the translation of Greek and Persian works. It remained the Abbasid seat until the Mongol sack of 1258.
dateNote: Al-Mansur began the city in 762.

title: Borobudur
summary: Borobudur is a vast Buddhist monument of terraces and bell-shaped stupas in central Java. It was built under the Sailendra dynasty around the late eighth and early ninth centuries. Reliefs around the galleries tell stories of the Buddha's former lives.
dateNote: Approximate. Construction is widely placed around 780–830.

title: Foundation of Angkor
summary: In 802 Jayavarman II was consecrated as a universal ruler, a date later Cambodian tradition treats as the start of the Khmer Empire. Angkor grew into a huge complex of temples and reservoirs. The city remained a capital for centuries.
dateNote: The consecration is traditionally dated to 802.

title: Heian capital
summary: In 794 the Japanese court moved to Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto. The city stayed the imperial capital for more than a thousand years. The Heian period is also the age of The Tale of Genji, written around the year 1000.
dateNote: The court moved in 794.

title: The Tale of Genji
summary: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji at the Heian court in the early eleventh century. It is often called the world's first novel. The exact years of composition are not known, but they fall in the 1000s.
dateNote: Approximate. The tale was written in the early eleventh century.

title: Movable type of Bi Sheng
summary: The Song-dynasty craftsman Bi Sheng made movable type from fired clay in the 1040s. Shen Kuo described the method in his Dream Pool Essays of 1088. Later printers in Korea and China developed metal type.
dateNote: Approximate. Shen Kuo places Bi Sheng's work in the Qingli era, 1041–1048.

title: First Crusade takes Jerusalem
summary: In July 1099 an army from western Europe captured Jerusalem after Pope Urban II's call to war in 1095. The attackers killed many of the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. Crusader states then held parts of the Levant for generations.
dateNote: Jerusalem was taken on 15 July 1099.

title: Genpei War
summary: The Taira and Minamoto clans fought a civil war from 1180 to 1185. The Minamoto victory at Dan-no-ura ended Taira power. Minamoto no Yoritomo then established the Kamakura shogunate.
dateNote: The war is dated from 1180 to 1185.

title: Delhi Sultanate
summary: In 1206 Qutb al-Din Aibak, a former slave general, became ruler in Delhi and began the Delhi Sultanate. Muslim dynasties then ruled much of northern India for three centuries. The Qutb Minar still marks the early capital.
dateNote: Aibak's rule in Delhi is dated from 1206.

title: Mongol conquests
summary: Temüjin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206 and his armies then conquered northern China, Central Asia, Iran, and parts of eastern Europe. The western campaigns reached Hungary in 1241. The line is a schematic of that westward thrust, not every front.
dateNote: Chinggis Khan was acclaimed in 1206. The campaign into Hungary was in 1241, and the empire's unity frayed after 1259.

title: Sack of Baghdad
summary: In 1258 Hülegü's Mongol army took Baghdad and killed the Abbasid caliph. The city's libraries and canals were devastated. The sack ended the Abbasid caliphate as a political power in Iraq.
dateNote: Baghdad fell in February 1258.

title: Mongol invasions of Japan
summary: Kublai Khan sent fleets against Japan in 1274 and 1281. Both were driven off, and a typhoon wrecked much of the second fleet. Japanese tradition called the storm a divine wind.
dateNote: The invasions are dated to 1274 and 1281.

title: Kublai Khan proclaims the Yuan
summary: Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279. He ruled China from Khanbaliq, on the site of modern Beijing. Marco Polo's book later described this court to European readers.
dateNote: The dynasty was proclaimed in 1271, and the Song fell in 1279.

title: Majapahit
summary: Majapahit arose in east Java in 1293 and became the leading kingdom of the Indonesian archipelago. Its influence is celebrated in the fourteenth-century poem Nagarakretagama. The capital faded in the early sixteenth century as Muslim ports rose.
dateNote: The kingdom is dated from 1293. Its decline is widely placed in the early 1500s.

title: Travels of Ibn Battuta
summary: Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 and travelled for nearly thirty years through Africa, the Middle East, India, Southeast Asia, and China. He dictated an account, the Rihla, after his return. It is a major eyewitness source for the fourteenth-century world.
dateNote: His travels are dated from 1325 to about 1354.

title: Foundation of Ayutthaya
summary: The kingdom of Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 on an island in the Chao Phraya River. It became a great trading power of mainland Southeast Asia. Burmese armies destroyed the city in 1767.
dateNote: The traditional foundation date is 1351.

title: Voyages of Zheng He
summary: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven fleets into the Indian Ocean, reaching Arabia and the East African coast. The ships carried diplomats, soldiers, and trade goods. The voyages stopped after his death and were not repeated on that scale.
dateNote: The seven voyages are dated from 1405 to 1433.

title: Promulgation of Hangul
summary: In 1446 King Sejong published Hunminjeongeum, the book that introduced the Korean alphabet now called Hangul. It was designed so that ordinary people could write their language. Classical Chinese remained the script of officials for centuries afterward.
dateNote: Hunminjeongeum was promulgated in 1446.

title: Ottoman conquest of Constantinople
summary: On 29 May 1453 Ottoman forces under Mehmed II took Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire. The city, later called Istanbul, became the Ottoman capital. Its fall closed the medieval Roman state in the east.
dateNote: The city fell on 29 May 1453.

title: First Battle of Panipat
summary: In 1526 Babur defeated the Delhi sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. He used field cannon and a cavalry practised on the steppe. The Mughal state then ruled much of India for three centuries.
dateNote: The battle was fought on 21 April 1526.

title: Imjin War
summary: Japanese armies under Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded Korea in 1592 and again after a brief truce. Korean naval victories led by Yi Sun-sin, and Ming Chinese intervention, forced a withdrawal by 1598. The war devastated the Korean peninsula.
dateNote: The invasions are dated from 1592 to 1598.

title: Battle of Sekigahara
summary: On 21 October 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated his rivals at Sekigahara. The victory let him establish the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603. That government ruled Japan until 1868.
dateNote: The battle was fought on 21 October 1600.

title: Taj Mahal
summary: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal. Work began in 1632 and the main mausoleum was finished in the early 1650s. It stands on the Yamuna at Agra.
dateNote: Construction began in 1632 and continued into the 1650s.

title: Qing take Beijing
summary: In 1644 a rebel army took Beijing and the last Ming emperor died. Manchu forces then entered the city and established the Qing dynasty. The Qing ruled China until 1912.
dateNote: Beijing changed hands in 1644.

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: On 23 June 1757 the East India Company under Robert Clive defeated the nawab of Bengal at Plassey. The victory, helped by a secret deal with the nawab's officers, began Company rule in Bengal. It was a turning point in the British conquest of India.
dateNote: The battle was fought on 23 June 1757.

title: Perry's mission to Japan
summary: In 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry brought United States warships into Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open ports. A treaty followed in 1854. The crisis weakened the Tokugawa government and led toward the Meiji Restoration.
dateNote: Perry arrived in July 1853. The Treaty of Kanagawa was signed in 1854.

title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
summary: In 1857 sepoys and a wide range of Indian rulers and towns rose against the East India Company. The fighting was fiercest in northern India and was put down by 1858. Britain then abolished the Company and ruled India directly.
dateNote: The uprising is dated from May 1857 to 1858.

title: Meiji Restoration
summary: In 1868 the Tokugawa shogunate fell and power was restored in the name of the emperor Meiji. The new government abolished the domains, built a conscript army, and industrialised. The capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo.
dateNote: The restoration is dated to January 1868.

title: First Sino-Japanese War
summary: War between Japan and Qing China in 1894–1895 was fought over Korea. Japan won, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki gave it Taiwan and influence in Korea. The result shifted the balance of power in East Asia.
dateNote: The war is dated from July 1894 to April 1895.

title: Xinhai Revolution
summary: An uprising at Wuchang in October 1911 spread through the provinces and ended the Qing dynasty. A republic was declared, and the last emperor abdicated in February 1912. Sun Yat-sen was briefly provisional president.
dateNote: The Wuchang uprising began on 10 October 1911.

title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
summary: On 13 April 1919 British-led troops fired on a crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. Several hundred people were killed. The massacre became a turning point in Indian opposition to colonial rule.
dateNote: The shooting was on 13 April 1919.

title: May Fourth Movement
summary: On 4 May 1919 students in Beijing protested the decision at Versailles to transfer German rights in Shandong to Japan. The protests grew into a wider call for cultural and political change. The movement is a landmark of modern Chinese nationalism.
dateNote: The Beijing demonstration was on 4 May 1919.

title: Nanjing Massacre
summary: After Japanese troops captured Nanjing in December 1937, they killed a very large number of civilians and prisoners and committed widespread rape. The killing continued for weeks. Estimates of the dead differ, and the massacre itself is documented by diaries, photographs, and the records of the Tokyo trials.
dateNote: The massacre followed the fall of Nanjing on 13 December 1937.

title: Partition of India
summary: In August 1947 British India became the independent states of India and Pakistan. Millions of people crossed the new borders, and communal killing took a very large, still disputed, number of lives. The partition remains central to the politics of South Asia.
dateNote: Independence and partition took effect on 14–15 August 1947.

title: People's Republic of China
summary: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. The Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan. The civil war's main campaigns on the mainland were over.
dateNote: The proclamation was on 1 October 1949.

title: Korean War
summary: War began on 25 June 1950 when North Korean forces invaded the South. United Nations forces, largely American, and later Chinese armies, fought until an armistice in 1953. No peace treaty was signed, and the peninsula stayed divided.
dateNote: The war is dated from 25 June 1950 to the armistice of 27 July 1953.

title: Battle of Dien Bien Phu
summary: Viet Minh forces defeated the French garrison at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954. The victory ended French colonial rule in Indochina. The Geneva conference that summer divided Vietnam temporarily at the 17th parallel.
dateNote: The garrison surrendered on 7 May 1954.

title: Great Leap Forward
summary: The Great Leap Forward of 1958 tried to industrialise China at great speed through communes and backyard steel. It was followed by a famine. Death tolls are estimated in the tens of millions, and the exact figure is disputed.
dateNote: The campaign and the famine are dated to 1958–1962.

title: Cultural Revolution
summary: In 1966 Mao Zedong launched the Cultural Revolution, and student Red Guards attacked officials, teachers, and historic sites. The turmoil lasted until Mao's death in 1976. It disrupted schools, families, and the Communist Party itself.
dateNote: The movement is dated from 1966 to 1976.

title: Iranian Revolution
summary: Mass protests in 1978–1979 overthrew the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile and an Islamic republic was declared. The revolution reshaped the politics of the Middle East.
dateNote: The shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, and the republic was declared on 1 April 1979.

title: Tiananmen Square protests
summary: In the spring of 1989 students and workers occupied Tiananmen Square calling for reform. On 3–4 June the army cleared Beijing by force, killing an unknown number of people. Public discussion of the crackdown is still censored in China.
dateNote: The military assault was on the night of 3–4 June 1989.

title: Handover of Hong Kong
summary: On 1 July 1997 Britain returned Hong Kong to China under an agreement that promised a separate system for fifty years. The handover ended more than 150 years of British rule. Later political conflict has tested that promise.
dateNote: The handover was at midnight on 1 July 1997.

title: Independence of Timor-Leste
summary: East Timor voted for independence from Indonesia in a 1999 referendum, after a long occupation. It became the state of Timor-Leste on 20 May 2002. Indonesian-backed militias had killed many civilians after the vote.
dateNote: Independence was restored on 20 May 2002.

title: Indian Ocean tsunami
place: Off the coast of Aceh, Indonesia
summary: On 26 December 2004 an earthquake off Sumatra caused a tsunami that killed more than 200,000 people around the Indian Ocean. Aceh was the worst hit. The disaster led to a large international relief effort.
dateNote: The earthquake was on 26 December 2004.

title: Egyptian uprising of 2011
summary: Protests in Cairo's Tahrir Square in January and February 2011 forced President Hosni Mubarak to resign. The uprising followed the revolution in Tunisia. The years after brought elections, a coup in 2013, and a return to strong military rule.
dateNote: Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011.

title: Expulsion of the Rohingya
summary: In August 2017 the Myanmar army drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims from Rakhine State into Bangladesh. Villages were burned and large numbers of civilians were killed. United Nations investigators later described the campaign as genocide.
dateNote: The main campaign began in late August 2017.

title: COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A new coronavirus was identified in Wuhan in late 2019 and spread worldwide. The World Health Organization described the outbreak as a pandemic in March 2020. It killed millions of people and shut down travel and daily life on every continent.
dateNote: The virus was first identified in Wuhan in December 2019. The pandemic declaration was on 11 March 2020.

title: Enuma Elish
summary: The Enuma Elish tells how Marduk defeated the sea Tiamat and built the world from her body. It is the great creation epic of Babylon. The classic form of the poem is known from tablets of the late second millennium BCE, and the story is older.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The standard Babylonian text is widely placed in the late second millennium BCE.

title: Epic of Gilgamesh
summary: Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk, is the hero of poems about friendship, the wilderness, and the search for eternal life. Sumerian tales about him were written down by about 2100 BCE. The famous standard Akkadian version is later.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Sumerian Gilgamesh poems were copied by about 2100 BCE. A traditional reign in the distant past is not a usable calendar date.

title: Inanna's descent
summary: In this Sumerian myth the goddess Inanna descends to the underworld, is killed, and is brought back. Old Babylonian tablets preserve the poem. It belongs to Uruk, her city.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The poem is known from Old Babylonian copies of about the nineteenth to seventeenth centuries BCE.

title: Ramayana
summary: The Ramayana tells of Rama's exile and the rescue of Sita from Lanka. Traditional sacred chronology places the story in a remote mythical age, not a historical century. The surviving epic was composed in the first millennium BCE and the early centuries CE.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Composition is widely placed between about 400 BCE and 200 CE. There is no agreed historical year for the tale.

title: Mahabharata
summary: The Mahabharata tells of a war between cousin clans on the field of Kurukshetra, and it includes the Bhagavad Gita. Its traditional setting is a heroic age without an agreed calendar date. The written epic grew between about 400 BCE and 400 CE.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The written epic grew over the centuries from about 400 BCE to 400 CE.

title: Dangun founds Gojoseon
summary: Korean tradition says that Dangun, born of a heavenly prince and a bear-woman, founded the first Korean kingdom in 2333 BCE. The story is a national origin myth, not a historical record. It was written down much later, notably in the thirteenth-century Samguk Yusa.
dateNote: Traditional date. The year 2333 BCE is the traditional founding date, recorded many centuries later.

title: Emperor Jimmu
summary: Japanese official tradition dated the accession of the first emperor, Jimmu, to 660 BCE. The tale, in which he descends from the sun goddess, is a foundation myth. It was set down in the Kojiki of 712 and the Nihon Shoki of 720.
dateNote: Traditional date. 660 BCE is the traditional accession year, written down in the eighth century.

title: Izanagi and Izanami
summary: The Kojiki tells how the creator couple Izanagi and Izanami stirred the sea and brought forth the Japanese islands. It is the oldest surviving Japanese book. The myths it records are older than the writing.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The Kojiki was completed in 712. The tradition is older.

title: Pangu separates heaven and earth
summary: Pangu is said to have grown inside a cosmic egg and then pushed heaven and earth apart. The written story is late compared with other Chinese myths. It is first attributed to Xu Zheng in the Three Kingdoms period.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The tale is credited to Xu Zheng in the third century CE.

title: Chang'e flies to the moon
summary: Chang'e is the goddess who flies to the moon after taking an elixir of immortality. The story is older than any single book, and a famous early telling is in the Huainanzi. That book was presented to the Han court in 139 BCE.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The Huainanzi, presented in 139 BCE, contains an early written telling.

title: Journey to the West
summary: Journey to the West turns the historical pilgrimage of the monk Xuanzang into a fantasy of demons, with the monkey king Sun Wukong as its hero. The novel was published in the sixteenth century. Xuanzang's real journey, in the seventh century, is a separate historical event.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The novel was published in the sixteenth century, traditionally in 1592.

title: Xuanzang's pilgrimage
summary: The monk Xuanzang left China in 629, travelled to India, and returned in 645 with Buddhist texts. His own Record of the Western Regions describes the kingdoms he saw. The novel Journey to the West later turned the journey into myth.
dateNote: He departed in 629 and returned in 645.

title: Trojan War
summary: Greek tradition tells of a Greek war against Troy to recover Helen, ending in the city's fall. Eratosthenes dated that fall to 1184 BCE. The Iliad is poetry, and a historical war on that scale is not established, though Troy was a real Late Bronze Age city.
dateNote: Traditional date. Eratosthenes placed the fall of Troy in 1184 BCE.

title: Bronze Age Troy
summary: The mound at Hisarlik was a fortified city through the Bronze Age, identified with the Troy of later Greek story. Several layers were destroyed, including one around 1180 BCE. Archaeology does not confirm the Homeric war, which is marked separately as myth.
dateNote: Approximate. Late Bronze Age Troy was occupied until destructions around 1180 BCE.

title: Petra
summary: Petra, carved into sandstone cliffs, was the capital of the Nabataean kingdom. Its monumental tombs and the treasury facade are widely dated around the first centuries BCE and CE. The city controlled caravan trade between Arabia and the Mediterranean.
dateNote: Approximate. The major monuments are widely dated around the turn of the era.

title: Homo sapiens at Bacho Kiro
summary: Teeth and bone fragments from Bacho Kiro are among the oldest widely accepted Homo sapiens remains in Europe. They are dated to about 45,000 years ago. The people there used ornaments and lived near the last Neanderthals.
dateNote: Approximate. The remains are dated to about 45,000 years ago.

title: Last Neanderthals
summary: Neanderthals disappeared from Europe around 40,000 years ago. Radiocarbon work led by Tom Higham places the last widely dated sites in that window. They left DNA in living people whose ancestors lived outside Africa.
dateNote: Approximate. The last European Neanderthals are widely dated to about 40,000 years ago.

title: Lion-man of Hohlenstein
summary: A mammoth-ivory figure with a human body and a lion's head was found in a cave on the Swabian Jura. It is dated to about 40,000 years ago. It is one of the oldest known statues.
dateNote: Approximate. The figure is dated to about 40,000 years ago.

title: Chauvet Cave
summary: Chauvet Cave holds paintings of lions, rhinos, and horses dated to about 36,000 to 33,000 years ago. The art is older than Lascaux by many millennia. The cave was sealed for most of later prehistory, which preserved the paintings.
dateNote: Approximate. The paintings are widely dated to about 36,000–33,000 years ago.

title: Venus of Willendorf
summary: A small limestone figure of a woman, found at Willendorf, is dated to about 29,500 years ago, around 27,500 BCE. It was carved and once painted during the last Ice Age. Its purpose is unknown.
dateNote: Approximate. The figurine is dated to about 29,500 years ago.

title: Last Glacial Maximum
summary: About 26,000 to 19,000 years ago, ice sheets reached their greatest recent extent across northern Europe and North America. Sea level was far lower, and people lived south of the ice. This pin marks the Fennoscandian sheet; the climate event was global.
dateNote: Approximate. The maximum is widely dated to about 26,000–19,000 years ago. The years stored here are the BCE equivalents.

title: Lascaux
summary: The paintings of horses, bulls, and deer at Lascaux are widely dated to about 17,000 BCE. The cave was found in 1940 and later closed to protect the art. A replica now receives visitors.
dateNote: Approximate. The paintings are widely dated to about 17,000 BCE.

title: Altamira
summary: The bison painted on the ceiling of Altamira are widely dated to the later Magdalenian, around 15,000 to 13,500 years ago. When the cave was found in the nineteenth century, many scholars refused to believe Ice Age people had made them. That doubt did not last.
dateNote: Approximate. The famous ceiling is widely dated to about 15,000–13,500 years ago.

title: Stonehenge
summary: An earthwork enclosure at Stonehenge began around 3000 BCE, and the great sarsen circle was raised around 2500 BCE. The stones were brought from Wales and from nearer quarries. The monument stayed in use for ceremonies and burials.
dateNote: Approximate. The enclosure begins around 3000 BCE and the sarsen circle around 2500 BCE.

title: Palace of Knossos
summary: Knossos was the largest palace of Minoan Crete, with courtyards, storerooms, and colourful frescoes. The first palaces rose around 1900 BCE. Later Greek myth placed the Minotaur here, which is a separate tradition from the archaeology.
dateNote: Approximate. The first palace phase is widely dated to about 1900 BCE.

title: Roman Republic
summary: Roman tradition dated the expulsion of the kings and the start of the Republic to 509 BCE. The state then expanded from a city to a Mediterranean power. It ended as a republic when Augustus established the principate in 27 BCE.
dateNote: The traditional start is 509 BCE. Augustus's settlement is dated to 27 BCE.

title: Battle of Marathon
summary: In 490 BCE an Athenian and Plataean army defeated a Persian landing force at Marathon. The battle stopped the first Persian invasion of mainland Greece. A second, larger invasion followed ten years later.
dateNote: The battle is dated to 490 BCE.

title: Battle of Salamis
summary: In 480 BCE Greek fleets defeated the Persian navy of Xerxes in the straits of Salamis. The victory followed the Persian sack of Athens and the stand at Thermopylae. It turned the second Persian invasion.
dateNote: The battle is dated to 480 BCE.

title: Trial of Socrates
summary: An Athenian jury condemned the philosopher Socrates to death in 399 BCE. Plato and Xenophon, his students, wrote accounts of the trial and of his last day. He was charged with impiety and with corrupting the young.
dateNote: The trial is dated to 399 BCE.

title: Assassination of Caesar
summary: On 15 March 44 BCE a group of senators stabbed Julius Caesar in the Theatre of Pompey. They claimed to be saving the Republic. Civil wars followed, and the Republic did not survive them.
dateNote: Caesar was killed on 15 March 44 BCE.

title: Eruption of Vesuvius
summary: In 79 CE Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pumice. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters written afterward. The buried cities preserve streets, houses, and bodies from a single day.
dateNote: The eruption is dated to 79 CE, traditionally 24 August, though some evidence points to the autumn.

title: Council of Nicaea
summary: In 325 the emperor Constantine called bishops to Nicaea to settle disputes about the nature of Christ. The council produced a creed that most later churches accepted in revised form. It was an imperial intervention in Christian doctrine.
dateNote: The council met in 325.

title: End of the western Roman Empire
summary: In 476 the soldier Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last western emperor, at Ravenna. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued. Later writers treated 476 as the end of the western Roman Empire, though the change was less sudden than that date suggests.
dateNote: Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476.

title: Reign of Justinian
summary: Justinian I ruled the eastern Roman Empire from 527 to 565. His lawyers produced the Corpus Juris Civilis, and Hagia Sophia was rebuilt after riots in 532. His armies retook parts of Italy and North Africa for a time.
dateNote: Justinian ruled from 527 to 565.

title: Raid on Lindisfarne
summary: In 793 a Viking fleet raided the monastery of Lindisfarne off the Northumbrian coast. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle treats the attack as a famous early blow of the Viking age in Britain. Raids and settlement then spread around the North Sea and the Atlantic.
dateNote: The raid is dated to 8 June 793.

title: Viking voyages west
summary: Norse sailors settled Iceland from about 870, Greenland from about 980, and reached Newfoundland around 1000. The site at L'Anse aux Meadows is the archaeological trace of that American landfall. The line is a schematic of the western route.
dateNote: Approximate. Iceland was settled from about 870, and the Newfoundland site dates to around 1000.

title: Coronation of Charlemagne
summary: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in St Peter's. Charlemagne already ruled the Franks and the Lombards from Aachen. The coronation revived an imperial title in the west.
dateNote: The coronation was on 25 December 800.

title: L'Anse aux Meadows
summary: Norse buildings at L'Anse aux Meadows are dated to around the year 1000. They are the only widely accepted Viking site in North America. The settlement was short-lived.
dateNote: Approximate. The occupation is widely dated to around 1000.

title: Norman conquest
summary: On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated King Harold at Hastings. William was crowned in Westminster Abbey that Christmas. The conquest replaced the English elite and tied England to northern France.
dateNote: The battle was fought on 14 October 1066.

title: Magna Carta
summary: In June 1215 rebel barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede. The charter limited some royal abuses and was reissued by later kings. A few of its clauses became famous in later arguments about law and liberty.
dateNote: The charter was sealed on 15 June 1215.

title: Black Death
summary: Plague reached Messina in 1347 and spread across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East within a few years. It killed a very large share of the population, widely estimated at around a third in Europe. The disease was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
dateNote: The European outbreak is dated from 1347 to about 1353.

title: Gutenberg Bible
summary: Johannes Gutenberg printed a Latin Bible at Mainz in the 1450s, using movable metal type. It is the first major European book printed this way. Printing then spread quickly across the continent.
dateNote: The Bible was completed around 1455.

title: Luther's theses
summary: In 1517 Martin Luther circulated ninety-five theses criticising indulgences. The protest, spread by print, began the Protestant Reformation. Luther was later outlawed by the emperor and protected by the elector of Saxony.
dateNote: The theses are dated to 31 October 1517.

title: De revolutionibus
summary: Nicolaus Copernicus's book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was published in 1543, the year he died. It set the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the planetary system. The idea spread slowly and was later defended by Galileo and Kepler.
dateNote: The book was published in 1543.

title: Spanish Armada
summary: In 1588 Philip II sent a fleet to escort an invasion of England. English ships and storms broke the Armada, and many of the surviving ships were wrecked on the voyage home around Scotland and Ireland. The defeat did not end the war.
dateNote: The campaign was in the summer of 1588.

title: Galileo's telescopic discoveries
summary: In 1610 Galileo Galilei published Sidereus Nuncius, describing mountains on the Moon and four moons orbiting Jupiter. He had seen them with a telescope he improved. The moons showed that not everything in the sky circled the Earth.
dateNote: Sidereus Nuncius was published in March 1610.

title: Newton's Principia
summary: Isaac Newton's Principia, published in 1687, set out the laws of motion and a universal law of gravitation. It explained the orbits of planets and the fall of objects with one theory. The book became the foundation of later physics.
dateNote: The Principia was published in 1687.

title: Lisbon earthquake
summary: On 1 November 1755 an earthquake and tsunami destroyed much of Lisbon and shook the western Mediterranean. Tens of thousands of people died. The disaster fed Enlightenment arguments about God, nature, and the duty of states to rebuild.
dateNote: The earthquake was on 1 November 1755.

title: Watt's steam engine
summary: James Watt patented a separate condenser for the steam engine in 1769, greatly improving earlier engines. With Matthew Boulton he began selling engines in the 1770s. The improved engine powered mines and, later, factories.
dateNote: The patent is dated 1769. Commercial engines followed in the 1770s.

title: French Revolution
summary: In 1789 the French Estates-General became a national assembly and a crowd stormed the Bastille. The revolution abolished feudal privileges, executed the king in 1793, and slid into the Terror and war. Napoleon took power in 1799.
dateNote: The revolution is dated from 1789. The coup of 18 Brumaire was in November 1799.

title: Revolutions of 1848
summary: In 1848 revolutions broke out from Paris to Vienna, Berlin, and Milan, demanding constitutions and national rights. Most of the uprisings were defeated within a year. They still ended serfdom in the Austrian Empire and spread liberal and nationalist politics.
dateNote: The main wave is dated to 1848–1849.

title: Unification of Italy
summary: The kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861 after the campaigns of Garibaldi and the house of Savoy. Venice joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870, when Italian troops entered the city. The Papal States then shrank to the Vatican.
dateNote: The kingdom was proclaimed on 17 March 1861. Rome was taken in 1870.

title: German Empire
summary: On 18 January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, after Prussia defeated France. Otto von Bismarck had united the German states under the Prussian king. The empire lasted until 1918.
dateNote: The empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871.

title: Berlin Conference
summary: From November 1884 to February 1885 European powers met in Berlin to set rules for claiming colonies in Africa. No African state was a party to the decisions. The conference sped the partition of the continent.
dateNote: The conference met from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885.

title: First World War
summary: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 began the July crisis and a continental war. The fighting killed about ten million soldiers and ended the Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian, and Ottoman empires. An armistice was signed on 11 November 1918.
dateNote: The war is dated from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.

title: Russian Revolution
summary: In February 1917 protests in Petrograd overthrew the tsar. In October the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, seized power from the provisional government. A civil war followed, and the Soviet state emerged from it.
dateNote: The two revolutions are dated to March and November 1917 in the modern calendar.

title: Second World War in Europe
summary: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war two days later. The war in Europe killed tens of millions of people and ended with Germany's surrender in May 1945. It was fought alongside the war in Asia and the Pacific.
dateNote: The European war is dated from 1 September 1939 to 8 May 1945.

title: The Holocaust
summary: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, and millions of Roma, disabled people, prisoners of war, and other civilians. Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest of the killing centres. The genocide is documented by German records, survivor testimony, and the sites themselves.
dateNote: The systematic murder is dated chiefly to 1941–1945.

title: Chernobyl disaster
summary: On 26 April 1986 a reactor at the Chernobyl nuclear plant exploded during a test. A radioactive cloud spread across Europe, and a large zone around the plant was abandoned. The disaster shook confidence in the Soviet system.
dateNote: The explosion was on 26 April 1986.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: On 9 November 1989 East German authorities opened the Berlin Wall, and crowds crossed freely. The wall had divided the city since 1961. German reunification followed in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
dateNote: The border opened on the night of 9 November 1989.

title: World Wide Web
summary: Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN, proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 and released it to the public in 1991. The web used hypertext links on top of the existing internet. It became the main public face of the network.
dateNote: The web was released outside CERN in 1991. The proposal is dated 1989.

title: Good Friday Agreement
summary: On 10 April 1998 the British and Irish governments and the Northern Irish parties signed the Good Friday Agreement. It set up power-sharing and a path to end the Troubles. Voters in Ireland, north and south, approved it in referendums.
dateNote: The agreement was signed on 10 April 1998.

title: Founding of Rome
summary: Roman tradition said the city was founded by Romulus on 21 April 753 BCE. The tale of the twins, the she-wolf, and the killing of Remus is myth. Archaeology shows villages on the Roman hills centuries earlier, without confirming that year.
dateNote: Traditional date. Later Roman writers placed the founding in 753 BCE.

title: Prometheus and Pandora
summary: Hesiod tells how Prometheus stole fire for humans and how Zeus sent Pandora, whose jar released evils into the world. The poems, the Theogony and Works and Days, are the earliest full written versions. They were composed around 700 BCE.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Hesiod's poems are widely dated to around 700 BCE.

title: Theseus and the Minotaur
summary: Athenian tradition made Theseus the hero who slew the Minotaur in the labyrinth of Crete and united Attica. There is no agreed historical year for his life. The story is fully visible in classical Athenian art and writing of the fifth century BCE.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The tale is well established in fifth-century BCE Athenian sources. No traditional calendar year is secure.

title: Beowulf
summary: Beowulf tells of a Geatish hero who kills the monster Grendel and, in old age, a dragon. The only surviving manuscript was written in England around the year 1000. The poem's story is set in Scandinavia and is older than that copy.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The surviving manuscript is dated to around 1000.

title: King Arthur
summary: Arthur appears as a British war leader in the ninth-century Historia Brittonum, and later medieval romances made him a king of a round table. There is no agreed historical date for his life, and a real Arthur is uncertain. The legend belongs to Britain and Brittany.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The Historia Brittonum, around 830, is the earliest substantial written mention.

title: Ragnarök
summary: Norse myth tells of Ragnarök, the last battle in which gods and giants kill one another and the world is remade. The fullest written versions are in the Icelandic Eddas. The Poetic Edda's main manuscript, the Codex Regius, is from about 1270.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The Codex Regius is dated to about 1270. The oral tradition is older.

title: The Táin
summary: The Táin Bó Cúailnge tells how the young hero Cú Chulainn defended Ulster against the armies of Connacht. It is the centre of the Irish Ulster Cycle. The oldest substantial manuscripts are from the twelfth century, and the stories are older.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The main manuscripts are medieval, from about the twelfth century.

title: Kalevala
summary: Elias Lönnrot compiled the Kalevala from Finnish and Karelian oral poems and published it in 1835, with a longer edition in 1849. It tells of the singer Väinämöinen and the smith Ilmarinen. The oral poems are older than the book.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Lönnrot's compilation was published in 1835 and enlarged in 1849.

title: The biblical flood
summary: Genesis tells of Noah, who survives a flood that covers the world. Related flood stories are older in Mesopotamia, and those are separate traditions. The biblical text as we have it was written down in the first millennium BCE.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The written Genesis flood is widely placed in the first millennium BCE. Mesopotamian flood poems are older and are not this text.

title: Peopling of the Americas
summary: People reached the Americas from north-east Asia while sea levels were low, and by about 14,500 years ago they were as far south as Chile. The widely accepted window for this spread is about 16,000 to 14,000 years ago. The line is a schematic through Beringia and down the continents. Earlier sites are still debated.
dateNote: Approximate. Widespread settlement is dated to about 16,000–14,000 years ago. The years stored here are the BCE equivalents.

title: Monte Verde
summary: Monte Verde, near Puerto Montt, was occupied about 14,500 years ago, around 12,500 BCE. Wooden remains, hearths, and tools survived in a bog. The site helped show that people were in South America before the Clovis culture.
dateNote: Approximate. The occupation is widely dated to about 14,500 years ago.

title: Clovis culture
summary: Clovis spear points, fluted and very widespread, date to about 13,000 years ago. They mark a famous early culture of North America, not the first people there. The culture lasted only a few centuries.
dateNote: Approximate. Clovis is widely dated to about 13,050–12,750 years ago.

title: Poverty Point
summary: Poverty Point is a set of enormous earth ridges built by hunter-gatherers in the lower Mississippi valley. The main earthworks are widely dated to about 1700–1100 BCE. People there traded stone from hundreds of kilometres away.
dateNote: Approximate. The earthworks are widely dated to about 1700–1100 BCE.

title: Olmec centres
summary: San Lorenzo and later La Venta were centres of the Olmec tradition, famous for colossal stone heads. San Lorenzo's peak is widely dated to about 1200–900 BCE. Olmec art and ritual influenced later Mesoamerican societies.
dateNote: Approximate. San Lorenzo flourished from about 1200 BCE.

title: City of Caral
summary: Caral, in the Supe Valley, is the oldest known city in the Americas, with plazas and pyramids. It flourished from about 3000 to 1800 BCE. The people farmed and fished, and they built on a monumental scale without pottery.
dateNote: Approximate. Caral is widely dated to about 3000–1800 BCE.

title: Chavín de Huántar
summary: Chavín de Huántar was a ceremonial centre in the Andes whose art spread widely. Its main temple phase is dated to about 900–200 BCE. A gallery inside the temple holds the Lanzón, a carved granite figure.
dateNote: Approximate. The horizon style is widely dated to about 900–200 BCE.

title: Early Maya writing
summary: Maya writing is in evidence by the Late Preclassic, around the last centuries BCE. It became a full hieroglyphic script used for history, ritual, and astronomy. Later Classic cities such as Tikal recorded long sequences of kings.
dateNote: Approximate. Early Maya script is widely placed by about the third century BCE.

title: Teotihuacan
summary: Teotihuacan grew into one of the largest cities in the world, with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon along a great avenue. Its height is widely dated from about 100 to 550. The city's violent burning in the sixth century ended its power.
dateNote: Approximate. The city's peak is widely dated to about 100–550.

title: Moche culture
place: Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, Peru
summary: The Moche of the north coast of Peru built adobe pyramids and made portrait vessels and fine metalwork. Their classic period is widely dated to about 100–700. Murals and pots show elaborate ceremonies, including sacrifice.
dateNote: Approximate. The Moche florescence is widely dated to about 100–700.

title: Nazca lines
summary: On the desert plain of Nazca, people scraped away dark stones to make huge figures and straight lines. Most of the geoglyphs are dated between about 200 BCE and 600 CE. They are best seen from above, though they were made and walked at ground level.
dateNote: Approximate. The lines are widely dated from about 200 BCE to 600 CE.

title: Yax K'uk' Mo' at Copán
summary: In 426 a ruler named Yax K'uk' Mo' founded the Classic dynasty of Copán, according to later inscriptions. The city became a major Maya centre of sculpture and astronomy. Its dated monuments run for centuries after that founding.
dateNote: The inscriptions date the founding to 426.

title: Tiwanaku
summary: Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, was the ceremonial capital of a highland state. Its monumental core flourished from about 500 to 1000. The Gateway of the Sun and huge stone blocks still stand on the site.
dateNote: Approximate. The monumental city is widely dated to about 500–1000.

title: Cahokia
summary: Around 1050, Cahokia near the Mississippi became the largest city north of Mexico, centred on Monks Mound. Its peak lasted into the twelfth century. The people, often linked to the Mississippian tradition, farmed maize and built plazas and mounds.
dateNote: Approximate. The city's sudden growth is widely dated to about 1050.

title: Chaco Canyon
summary: In Chaco Canyon, Ancestral Puebloans built great houses such as Pueblo Bonito and a network of roads. The classic period is widely dated to about 850–1150. The canyon was a ceremonial centre for a wide region of the Southwest.
dateNote: Approximate. The great-house era is widely dated to about 850–1150.

title: Thule migration
summary: Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, spread east from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland around 1000–1300. They used dog sleds, umiaks, and toggling harpoons. They replaced or absorbed the earlier Dorset tradition.
dateNote: Approximate. The eastward spread is widely dated to about 1000–1300.

title: Foundation of Tenochtitlan
summary: Mexica tradition dates the founding of Tenochtitlan, on islands in Lake Texcoco, to 1325. The city became the capital of the Aztec Empire. Spanish forces and indigenous allies destroyed it in 1521.
dateNote: The traditional foundation date is 1325.

title: Inca expansion
summary: From the reign of Pachacuti, traditionally beginning in 1438, the Inca state expanded from Cusco into the largest empire of the Americas. It built roads, storehouses, and the estate of Machu Picchu. Spanish forces captured the emperor Atahualpa in 1532.
dateNote: Pachacuti's reign is traditionally dated from 1438. Atahualpa was captured in 1532.

title: Columbus reaches the Caribbean
summary: On 12 October 1492 a Spanish expedition led by Christopher Columbus landed in the Bahamas, after crossing the Atlantic from Palos. He thought he was near Asia. The voyage began sustained European colonisation of the Americas, with catastrophic consequences for indigenous peoples.
dateNote: Landfall was on 12 October 1492.

title: Cabral reaches Brazil
summary: On 22 April 1500 a Portuguese fleet under Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted the coast of Brazil. Portugal then claimed the land under the Treaty of Tordesillas. The landing began Portuguese colonisation of South America.
dateNote: The landfall is dated to 22 April 1500.

title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: Hernán Cortés landed on the Mexican coast in 1519 and, with many indigenous allies, reached Tenochtitlan. Disease, siege, and war destroyed the Aztec capital in 1521. Spanish colonial rule of central Mexico followed.
dateNote: Cortés landed in 1519. Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521.

title: Spanish capture of the Inca emperor
summary: In November 1532 Francisco Pizarro's small force seized the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Atahualpa was killed in 1533 after a huge ransom in gold and silver. Spanish rule then spread through the Andes.
dateNote: Atahualpa was seized on 16 November 1532 and killed in 1533.

title: Silver of Potosí
summary: Silver was found at Potosí in 1545, and the mountain became the richest mine of the Spanish Empire. Forced and wage labour, including the mita draft, pulled indigenous people into deadly work. American silver reshaped prices from Seville to China.
dateNote: The discovery is dated to 1545.

title: Atlantic slave trade
