summary: From the sixteenth century into the nineteenth, European ships carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database records about 12.5 million people forced onto ships. The trade enriched European and American ports and devastated societies in Africa.
dateNote: Approximate. A direct trade to the Spanish Caribbean was licensed in 1518, and voyages continued into the 1860s.

title: Pueblo Revolt
summary: In 1680 Pueblo communities led by Popé drove Spanish colonists out of New Mexico. The revolt answered forced labour and the suppression of Pueblo religion. Spain reconquered the region in the 1690s.
dateNote: The revolt began on 10 August 1680.

title: Haitian Revolution
summary: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in 1791. Under leaders including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeated French, Spanish, and British forces. Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804, the first state born of a successful revolt of enslaved people.
dateNote: The revolt began in August 1791. Independence was declared on 1 January 1804.

title: Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II
summary: In 1780 José Gabriel Condorcanqui, called Túpac Amaru II, led a great Andean rebellion against Spanish officials. The rising spread through the southern Andes and was crushed in 1781. He was executed in Cusco.
dateNote: The rebellion is dated from November 1780 to 1781.

title: Battle of Ayacucho
summary: On 9 December 1824 a patriot army under Antonio José de Sucre defeated the last large Spanish force in Peru at Ayacucho. The battle ended Spanish rule on the South American mainland. Bolívar's campaigns had prepared the victory.
dateNote: The battle was fought on 9 December 1824.

title: Independence of Brazil
summary: On 7 September 1822 Prince Pedro declared Brazil independent of Portugal on the banks of the Ipiranga. He became emperor Pedro I. Brazil, unlike most of Spanish America, remained a monarchy for the rest of the century.
dateNote: Independence was declared on 7 September 1822.

title: Indian Removal
summary: The United States Indian Removal Act of 1830 authorised the expulsion of eastern nations to lands west of the Mississippi. In 1838 the army forced the Cherokee west on a journey remembered as the Trail of Tears. Thousands died on the removals.
dateNote: The Act is dated 1830. The Cherokee removal was in 1838.

title: Cherokee syllabary
summary: Sequoyah completed a syllabary for the Cherokee language in 1821, and it was quickly adopted. Within a few years Cherokee people were printing books and a newspaper in their own script. It is a rare case of a writing system invented by one person and taken up by a nation.
dateNote: The syllabary was completed in 1821.

title: Independence of Mexico
summary: After a war that began with Miguel Hidalgo's call in 1810, Mexico won independence in 1821 under the Plan of Iguala. Agustín de Iturbide entered Mexico City in September. Spain's three-century viceroyalty of New Spain was over.
dateNote: The Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821.

title: United States Civil War
summary: Eleven southern states seceded in 1860–1861 to protect slavery, and war followed until 1865. The Union victory ended legal slavery through the Thirteenth Amendment. About 750,000 soldiers died, and the Reconstruction that followed was bitterly contested.
dateNote: The war is dated from April 1861 to April 1865. The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in December 1865.

title: Canadian Confederation
summary: On 1 July 1867 the British North America Act joined Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick as the Dominion of Canada. Other provinces and territories entered later. Indigenous nations were not partners to the Act.
dateNote: Confederation took effect on 1 July 1867.

title: War of the Pacific
summary: Chile fought Bolivia and Peru from 1879 to 1884 over the nitrate deserts of the Atacama. Chile won and took territories that left Bolivia landlocked. The war still shapes relations among the three countries.
dateNote: The war is dated from 1879 to the Treaty of Ancón's aftermath in 1884.

title: Abolition in Brazil
summary: The Golden Law of 13 May 1888 abolished slavery in Brazil, the last country in the Americas to do so. Princess Isabel signed it in the absence of the emperor. The monarchy itself fell the next year.
dateNote: The Golden Law was signed on 13 May 1888.

title: Mexican Revolution
summary: In 1910 Francisco Madero challenged the long rule of Porfirio Díaz, and the country slid into revolution. Leaders including Emiliano Zapata and Pancho Villa fought over land and power. A new constitution in 1917, and the end of major fighting around 1920, reshaped the state.
dateNote: The revolution is dated from 1910. The constitution is of 1917.

title: Panama Canal
summary: The Panama Canal opened to shipping on 15 August 1914, linking the Atlantic and Pacific. The United States had backed Panama's separation from Colombia in 1903 and then built the canal. Thousands of workers, many from the Caribbean, died during construction.
dateNote: The canal opened on 15 August 1914.

title: Tulsa massacre
summary: On 31 May and 1 June 1921 a white mob destroyed the Black district of Greenwood in Tulsa. Hundreds of people were killed and thousands were left homeless. The attack was long minimised in official accounts.
dateNote: The massacre was on 31 May–1 June 1921.

title: Dust Bowl
summary: In the 1930s drought and ploughing turned the southern plains of the United States into the Dust Bowl. Huge storms stripped the soil, and many farm families left. The crisis coincided with the Great Depression.
dateNote: The worst dust storms are dated to the 1930s.

title: New Deal
summary: After taking office in 1933, Franklin Roosevelt launched the New Deal, a set of relief, recovery, and reform programmes. It included public works, banking reform, and Social Security. It did not end the Depression by itself, but it remade the federal government.
dateNote: Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933. Major New Deal laws followed through the 1930s.

title: Cuban Revolution
summary: On 1 January 1959 Fidel Castro's rebel movement took power in Cuba after the flight of Fulgencio Batista. The new government broke with the United States and aligned with the Soviet Union. The revolution reshaped the Caribbean and the Cold War.
dateNote: Batista fled on 1 January 1959.

title: Civil Rights Act
summary: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed segregation in public places and discrimination in employment in the United States. It followed the March on Washington in 1963 and years of Black organising. President Lyndon Johnson signed it on 2 July 1964.
dateNote: The Act was signed on 2 July 1964.

title: Apollo 11
summary: Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July 1969, and on 20 July Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon. Michael Collins stayed in orbit. It was the first time people landed on another world.
dateNote: Launch was on 16 July 1969. The landing was on 20 July 1969.

title: Coup in Chile
summary: On 11 September 1973 the Chilean armed forces overthrew President Salvador Allende, who died in the presidential palace. General Augusto Pinochet then ruled as a dictator until 1990. Thousands of people were killed or tortured.
dateNote: The coup was on 11 September 1973.

title: Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
summary: From April 1977 mothers of people kidnapped by Argentina's military dictatorship marched each week in the Plaza de Mayo. They demanded to know where their children were. The marches became the most visible protest against the junta.
dateNote: The first march was on 30 April 1977.

title: Chilean plebiscite
summary: On 5 October 1988 Chileans voted No to another term for Augusto Pinochet. The vote, which the regime had expected to win, opened the way to elections. Pinochet left the presidency in 1990.
dateNote: The plebiscite was on 5 October 1988.

title: Colombian peace agreement
summary: In 2016 the Colombian government and the FARC guerrilla army signed a peace agreement ending a war that had lasted more than fifty years. A first text was narrowly rejected in a referendum, and a revised accord was then approved by Congress. The conflict had killed hundreds of thousands of people.
dateNote: The final agreement was signed on 24 November 2016.

title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada
summary: In 2015 Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported on residential schools, which had removed indigenous children from their families for more than a century. The commission called the system a cultural genocide. Its calls to action remain a reference point in Canadian politics.
dateNote: The final report was released on 15 December 2015.

title: Popol Vuh
summary: The Popol Vuh tells how the Hero Twins defeated the lords of the underworld, and how the K'iche' people were created. It is the great written myth of the K'iche' Maya. The alphabetic text was set down in the 1550s, from an older tradition, and later copied by the friar Francisco Ximénez.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The alphabetic Popol Vuh was written in the 1550s. The tradition is older.

title: The Fifth Sun
summary: Aztec tradition held that the present world is the Fifth Sun, made when gods sacrificed themselves at Teotihuacan. The story was painted in pre-Hispanic books and written in Spanish and Nahuatl after the conquest. The fullest alphabetic accounts date to the mid-sixteenth century.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Alphabetic accounts were written in the mid-sixteenth century. Painted books are older, and their exact years are not fixed.

title: Quetzalcoatl
summary: Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, is a major sacred figure of Mesoamerica, linked both to a god and to stories of a priest-king of Tollan. There is no single agreed historical year for those stories. They were written down in Spanish and Nahuatl chronicles of the sixteenth century, and they appear in earlier art.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The narrative was written in sixteenth-century chronicles. Images of the feathered serpent are much older.

title: Viracocha
summary: Inca tradition told of Viracocha, a creator who travelled the world and of the first ancestors who emerged near Cusco. Spanish chroniclers wrote these stories down in the sixteenth century. There is no traditional calendar year that historians treat as a date for the creation itself.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Spanish chronicles of the mid-sixteenth century are the earliest full texts. The tradition is older.

title: El Dorado
summary: Spanish writers turned reports of a Muisca ritual, in which a ruler covered in gold dust offered treasure to Lake Guatavita, into the legend of a golden kingdom. The written legend is a sixteenth-century European story about an American rite. Expeditions spent decades looking for a city that was not there.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Spanish accounts of the gilded king were written in the sixteenth century.

title: Raven releases the light
summary: Haida, Tlingit, and other Northwest Coast traditions tell how Raven stole the sun, moon, and stars from a box and released them. The stories were oral long before anyone wrote them down. Substantial written versions were recorded by ethnographers around the end of the nineteenth century.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Extended written versions were recorded around 1890–1910. The oral tradition is older.

title: Muisca gold raft
summary: Muisca communities around the high lakes of Colombia made gold offerings, including the famous gold raft now in Bogotá. The ritual tradition is dated to the centuries before the Spanish conquest. Spanish observers later turned one ceremony into the legend of El Dorado.
dateNote: Approximate. Muisca goldwork and lake offerings are dated to the late pre-Hispanic centuries.

title: Haitian constitution of 1805
summary: In 1805 independent Haiti adopted a constitution under Jean-Jacques Dessalines. It abolished slavery and claimed the land for all Haitians. The document followed the declaration of independence of 1804.
dateNote: The constitution is dated 20 May 1805.

title: War of the Triple Alliance
summary: From 1864 to 1870 Paraguay fought Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. The war killed a huge part of Paraguay's population, though exact figures are disputed. It remains the most destructive interstate war in South American history.
dateNote: The war is dated from 1864 to 1870.

title: Amazon rubber boom
summary: From about 1880 to 1912 a boom in wild rubber made Manaus rich and pulled indigenous people into violent labour across the Amazon. The opera house in Manaus is a monument of that boom. Plantations in Asia then undercut the trade.
dateNote: Approximate. The boom is widely dated from about 1880 to 1912.

title: Falklands War
summary: In April 1982 Argentina seized the Falkland Islands, which it calls the Malvinas and which Britain had long administered. Britain retook the islands in a war that ended in June. The sovereignty dispute was not settled.
dateNote: Argentine forces landed on 2 April 1982. Fighting ended on 14 June 1982.

title: Stonewall uprising
summary: On 28 June 1969 patrons of the Stonewall Inn in New York resisted a police raid. Several nights of protest followed. The uprising became a symbol of the movement for gay and transgender rights.
dateNote: The raid was on 28 June 1969.

title: Attacks of 11 September 2001
summary: On 11 September 2001 hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania. Nearly three thousand people were killed. The attacks began a long war led by the United States.
dateNote: The attacks were on 11 September 2001.

title: Election of Barack Obama
summary: In November 2008 Barack Obama was elected president of the United States, the first Black person to hold the office. He took office in January 2009 during a global financial crisis. His election did not end racial inequality.
dateNote: The election was on 4 November 2008.

title: Wari Empire
summary: The Wari state, based near Ayacucho, built planned compounds across much of Peru. It flourished from about 600 to 1000, alongside Tiwanaku in the south. Its collapse left the highlands divided before the Inca expansion.
dateNote: Approximate. Wari is widely dated to about 600–1000.

title: Settlement of Sahul
summary: People had reached Sahul, the Ice Age continent of Australia and New Guinea, by about 50,000 years ago. Excavations at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land have been dated to about 65,000 years ago, a result that is widely cited and still discussed. The crossing from Island Southeast Asia required boats.
dateNote: Approximate. Settlement by about 50,000 years ago is widely accepted. Madjedbebe has been dated to about 65,000.

title: Kimberley rock art
summary: The Kimberley holds vast bodies of rock art, including the elegant Gwion figures. Some of that art is widely placed in the late Ice Age, around 12,000 years ago, and other paintings are much younger or still hard to date. The art belongs to Aboriginal traditions that continue.
dateNote: Approximate. Some Kimberley paintings are widely placed around 12,000 years ago, and many dates remain uncertain.

title: Austronesian voyages
summary: Speakers of Austronesian languages left Taiwan around 3000 BCE and settled the Philippines, Indonesia, and Near Oceania. Archaeology and language both trace this expansion. The line is a schematic of the early voyaging, which later carried people into the remote Pacific and to Madagascar.
dateNote: Approximate. The expansion from Taiwan is widely dated to about 3000–1500 BCE.

title: Lapita settlement of Remote Oceania
summary: People making dentate-stamped Lapita pottery sailed beyond the Solomon Islands into Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa. That leap into Remote Oceania is widely dated to about 1100–800 BCE. It was the base from which later Polynesian cultures grew.
dateNote: Approximate. Lapita in Remote Oceania is widely dated to about 1100–800 BCE.

title: Polynesian settlement of the eastern Pacific
place: Samoa to the Society Islands and Rapa Nui
summary: Polynesian navigators settled the Society Islands, Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui, and Aotearoa between about 900 and 1300. They sailed double canoes by stars, swells, and birds. The line sketches one eastern route, from Samoa toward Tahiti and Rapa Nui.
dateNote: Approximate. Eastern Polynesia was settled between about 900 and 1300.

title: Settlement of Hawaiʻi
summary: Polynesian voyagers settled the Hawaiian islands around 1000–1200. They brought crops, animals, and a language closely related to Māori and Tahitian. Later Hawaiian kingdoms grew from those founding communities.
dateNote: Approximate. Settlement is widely dated to about 1000–1200.

title: Settlement of Aotearoa
summary: Polynesian navigators settled Aotearoa New Zealand in the late thirteenth century. Radiocarbon dates and the extinction of the moa cluster around 1250–1300. Māori traditions remember the voyaging canoes that made the crossing.
dateNote: Approximate. Settlement is widely dated to about 1250–1300.

title: Settlement of Rapa Nui
summary: Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island, was settled by Polynesian voyagers around 1200. Older claims of a much earlier date have not held. The islanders later carved the moai, the great stone figures.
dateNote: Approximate. Current dating places settlement around 1200.

title: Moai of Rapa Nui
summary: Between about 1250 and 1500, people on Rapa Nui carved and raised hundreds of moai. The statues stood on stone platforms and faced inland over clan lands. Making and moving them required a large, organised community.
dateNote: Approximate. The main period of moai is widely dated to about 1250–1500.

title: Settlement of Madagascar
summary: Madagascar was settled by people from Island Southeast Asia, with African communities joining them. Linguistic and genetic evidence places the main Austronesian arrival between about 500 and 1000. Malagasy is an Austronesian language with African influences.
dateNote: Approximate. The Austronesian settlement is widely placed between about 500 and 1000.

title: Cook's Pacific voyages
summary: James Cook's three voyages between 1768 and 1779 mapped much of the Pacific, including the east coast of Australia and Hawaiʻi. He was killed at Kealakekua Bay in 1779. The voyages opened the ocean to later European colonisation.
dateNote: The voyages are dated from 1768 to Cook's death on 14 February 1779.

title: Kamehameha unites Hawaiʻi
summary: By 1810 Kamehameha I had brought the Hawaiian islands under one kingdom, after years of war. He used traditional alliances and European ships and guns. The kingdom lasted until the overthrow of 1893.
dateNote: The islands were united by 1810.

title: Treaty of Waitangi
summary: On 6 February 1840 Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed the Treaty of Waitangi. The English and Māori texts do not say the same thing about sovereignty. The treaty is the founding document of the New Zealand state, and it remains disputed.
dateNote: The treaty was first signed on 6 February 1840.

title: New Zealand Wars
summary: Wars between the Crown and Māori communities ran, with pauses, from 1845 to 1872. Large areas of Māori land were confiscated afterward. The fighting included the Waikato War of 1863–1864.
dateNote: The wars are dated from 1845 to 1872.

title: Nuclear tests at Bikini Atoll
summary: The United States tested nuclear weapons at Bikini Atoll from 1946 to 1958, after removing the islanders. The 1954 Castle Bravo test was far larger than planned and irradiated the crew of a Japanese fishing boat and people on other atolls. Bikini remains largely uninhabitable.
dateNote: Tests ran from 1946 to 1958. Castle Bravo was on 1 March 1954.

title: Federation of Australia
summary: On 1 January 1901 the six Australian colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia. Indigenous Australians were excluded from the new political settlement. Canberra later became the capital.
dateNote: Federation took effect on 1 January 1901.

title: Gallipoli campaign
summary: In 1915 Allied forces, including large Australian and New Zealand contingents, landed at Gallipoli and failed to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war. Both sides suffered very heavy casualties before the Allies withdrew. The campaign became a national story in Australia, New Zealand, and Turkey.
dateNote: The landings were on 25 April 1915. The evacuation ended in January 1916.

title: Independence of Samoa
summary: Western Samoa became independent of New Zealand on 1 January 1962, the first Pacific island country to do so in that era. It later renamed itself the Independent State of Samoa. American Samoa remained a United States territory.
dateNote: Independence was on 1 January 1962.

title: Independence of Fiji
summary: Fiji became independent of Britain on 10 October 1970. The new state inherited a divided politics between indigenous Fijians and the descendants of Indian indentured labourers. Later coups showed how unsettled that settlement was.
dateNote: Independence was on 10 October 1970.

title: Independence of Papua New Guinea
summary: Papua New Guinea became independent of Australia on 16 September 1975. It is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world. The state joined a highland interior to coastal and island societies.
dateNote: Independence was on 16 September 1975.

title: Sinking of the Rainbow Warrior
summary: On 10 July 1985 French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour, killing the photographer Fernando Pereira. The ship had been preparing to protest French nuclear tests at Moruroa. France later admitted responsibility.
dateNote: The bombing was on 10 July 1985.

title: Mabo decision
summary: In 1992 the High Court of Australia recognised native title in the Mabo case, brought by Eddie Mabo and others from Mer in the Torres Strait. The decision rejected the idea that Australia had been empty land at colonisation. A Native Title Act followed in 1993.
dateNote: The judgment was handed down on 3 June 1992.

title: Māui fishes up islands
summary: Māori tradition tells how the ancestor Māui fished the North Island out of the sea from his canoe. The story is much older than writing in Aotearoa. Sir George Grey published a major written collection of these traditions in 1854.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Grey's Polynesian Mythology was published in 1854. The oral tradition is far older.

title: Pele
summary: Pele is the volcano goddess of Hawaiʻi, at home in Kīlauea, and chants tell of her journey from Kahiki. The tradition is older than any book. Missionaries and Hawaiian writers set down versions in the early nineteenth century.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Written versions were recorded in the early nineteenth century. The tradition is older.

title: Kumulipo
summary: The Kumulipo is a Hawaiian chant of creation, composed for an eighteenth-century chief and later written down. It traces life from the coral polyp to the royal line. A famous published text appeared in the nineteenth century, long after the chant existed.
dateNote: Earliest written source. The chant belongs to the eighteenth century and was published in writing in the nineteenth. It records an older cosmology.

title: Arrernte ancestral narratives written down
summary: Arrernte and neighbouring peoples tell of ancestral beings who formed the country. Those traditions are vastly older than European contact. Spencer and Gillen's Native Tribes of Central Australia, published in 1899, was an early extended written record, not the beginning of the stories.
dateNote: Earliest written source. Spencer and Gillen published in 1899. The oral tradition is far older.

title: Cook crosses the Antarctic Circle
summary: On 17 January 1773 James Cook's Resolution crossed the Antarctic Circle, the first ship known to have done so. He circumnavigated the ice but did not sight the continent for certain. His voyage disproved the idea of a habitable southern continent reaching into temperate seas.
dateNote: The crossing was on 17 January 1773.

title: Sightings of Antarctica
summary: In 1820 several expeditions saw the Antarctic ice coast. The Russian ships of Bellingshausen and Lazarev, and British and American sealers including Bransfield and Palmer, were all in those waters. No single 'first sighting' is undisputed, but the continent was seen that year.
dateNote: The sightings are dated to 1820.

title: Amundsen reaches the South Pole
summary: On 14 December 1911 Roald Amundsen and four companions reached the South Pole. They had set out from the Bay of Whales with dogsleds. They returned safely to their base.
dateNote: The party reached the pole on 14 December 1911.

title: Scott at the South Pole
summary: Robert Falcon Scott's party reached the South Pole on 17 January 1912 and found that Amundsen had been there first. All five men died on the return journey across the Ross Ice Shelf. Their diaries were found with the bodies the next summer.
dateNote: Scott reached the pole on 17 January 1912.

title: Antarctic Treaty
summary: Twelve countries signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington on 1 December 1959. It set the continent aside for peaceful science and froze territorial claims. The treaty followed the International Geophysical Year of 1957–1958.
dateNote: The treaty was signed on 1 December 1959.

title: Antarctic ozone hole
summary: In 1985 scientists from the British Antarctic Survey reported a deep springtime loss of ozone over Antarctica. The hole was linked to chlorofluorocarbons. The finding led to the Montreal Protocol of 1987, which phased those chemicals out.
dateNote: The paper was published in May 1985.

title: EPICA Dome C ice core
summary: In 2004 the European EPICA project finished drilling an ice core at Dome C that reached about 800,000 years of climate history. The core records repeated ice ages in trapped air and ice. It is a basic archive for the climate of the last several hundred thousand years.
dateNote: The bedrock drilling was completed in 2004.

title: Collapse of Larsen B
summary: In early 2002 the Larsen B ice shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula collapsed over a few weeks. About 3,250 square kilometres of ice broke apart. The collapse followed strong regional warming and became a symbol of Antarctic change.
dateNote: The collapse was observed in January and March 2002.

title: Kīngitanga
summary: In 1858 Māori leaders installed Pōtatau Te Wherowhero as the first Māori king. The Kīngitanga was meant to unite tribes and hold land against colonial sale. It became a lasting institution, still based at Tūrangawaewae.
dateNote: Pōtatau was raised up as king in 1858.

title: French tests at Moruroa
summary: France tested nuclear weapons at Moruroa and Fangataufa from 1966 to 1996, first in the air and later underground. Pacific governments and protest voyages opposed the tests. France ended them in 1996 after a final series and worldwide criticism.
dateNote: Atmospheric and underground tests ran from 1966 to 1996.

title: Handback of Uluru
summary: On 26 October 1985 the Australian government returned the title of Uluru to its Anangu traditional owners, who leased it back as a national park. The handback recognised a sacred place that had been taken for tourism. Climbing the rock was later banned.
dateNote: The handback was on 26 October 1985.

title: Moriori of Rēkohu
summary: Polynesian voyagers settled Rēkohu, the Chatham Islands, around 1500 and became the Moriori. They lived by a code that limited warfare. In 1835 Māori groups from Taranaki invaded and killed or enslaved many Moriori, a later and separate event.
dateNote: Approximate. Settlement is widely dated to about 1500.

title: Kuk Swamp agriculture
summary: At Kuk Swamp in the New Guinea highlands, drainage ditches and plant remains show early agriculture. The evidence is widely dated to about 7000–5000 BCE, and some features may be older. Highland New Guinea was an independent centre of plant domestication.
dateNote: Approximate. Early cultivation at Kuk is widely dated to about 7000–5000 BCE.

title: Domestication of maize
summary: Maize was domesticated from the wild grass teosinte in the Balsas valley of south-western Mexico. The process was gradual and was underway by about 7000 BCE. Maize later became the staple of much of the Americas.
dateNote: Approximate. Domestication was underway by about 7000 BCE.

title: Andean potatoes
summary: People in the Andes domesticated the potato and other highland crops. Archaeological potatoes are widely dated to about 5000–3000 BCE. The crop later spread worldwide after the Spanish conquest.
dateNote: Approximate. Domesticated potatoes are widely in evidence by about 5000–3000 BCE.

title: Domestication of the dog
summary: Dogs are the first domesticated animal, descended from wolves. The place and the century are still debated, and estimates range from about 15,000 to more than 30,000 years ago. By the end of the Ice Age, dogs were living with people in Eurasia.
dateNote: Approximate. Dates differ by many thousands of years. A widely discussed range falls in the late Ice Age.

title: Start of the Holocene
summary: About 11,700 years ago the Earth left the last glacial period and entered the Holocene, the warm epoch of farming and cities. The boundary is defined in a Greenland ice core. Sea levels rose for millennia afterward as the ice sheets melted.
dateNote: Approximate. The Holocene boundary is dated to about 11,700 years ago, around 9700 BCE.

title: Younger Dryas
summary: The Younger Dryas was a sharp return of cold lasting from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago. It interrupted the warming at the end of the Ice Age, and it is recorded in ice cores and lake beds around the North Atlantic. Its cause is still discussed.
dateNote: Approximate. The cold interval is dated to about 12,900–11,700 years ago.

title: Natufian communities
summary: Natufian communities in the Levant built more permanent settlements and harvested wild cereals before full farming. They are widely dated to about 13,000–9,500 BCE. Some of the earliest known bread and beer come from this world.
dateNote: Approximate. The Natufian is widely dated to about 13,000–9,500 BCE.

title: Ain Mallaha
summary: Ain Mallaha is a Natufian settlement with stone houses and a famous burial of a person with a dog. It was occupied around 12,000–10,000 BCE. The site shows village life beginning before agriculture was complete.
dateNote: Approximate. The settlement is widely dated to about 12,000–10,000 BCE.

title: City of Uruk
summary: Uruk grew into the first great city of Mesopotamia in the fourth millennium BCE, with monumental temples and tens of thousands of people. Writing appeared there near the end of this period. The city gives its name to the Uruk period.
dateNote: Approximate. The Uruk period is widely dated to about 4000–3100 BCE.

title: Early Egyptian hieroglyphs
summary: Labels from royal tombs at Abydos show Egyptian hieroglyphs by about 3200 BCE. They name early kings and goods. Egyptian writing arose around the same centuries as Mesopotamian writing, and the two systems are distinct.
dateNote: Approximate. The earliest hieroglyphic labels are widely dated to about 3200–3000 BCE.
